title: Wound Culture, Pseudomonas Clues and the AmpC Trap
summary: Sample tissue instead of a surface swab, recognise Pseudomonas aeruginosa on the bench and in a puncture wound, and see which of the SPACE organisms really derepress AmpC during cephalosporin therapy.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 57 Hits 12, 24, 26 and 42, checked against Tamma 2019 (AmpC primer; read via a page-fetch tool), Behzadi 2021, Pachori 2019, Nelson 2018 (CODIFI) and Thakolkaran 2019 (read via a page-fetch tool; a direct download of that page hit a browser check). Hit 12 asks for all SPACE organisms to be treated as resistant to extended-spectrum cephalosporins; Tamma 2019 concentrates that risk in Enterobacter spp. and K. aerogenes, says treatment of the other SPACE organisms can follow in vitro susceptibility, classes Acinetobacter baumannii chromosomal resistance as noninducible, and gives treatment advice for Enterobacterales only (register flag rv-space-ampc-blanket). Hit 42’s “never a surface swab” is qualified: a Levine-technique swab still reported a pathogen in 70.1% of infected diabetic foot ulcers, against 86.1% for tissue, and tissue sampling caused more pain and bleeding (register flag rv-wound-swab-levine). Hit 26 names only P. aeruginosa for a sneaker-sole puncture wound; Thakolkaran 2019 lists S. aureus and P. aeruginosa for puncture wounds (register flag rv-puncture-two-organisms). Not taught as fact: the sneaker-insole reservoir, aspirates as a specimen choice, the pathogen-by-site map, antibiotic regimens beyond the AmpC discussion, carbapenemase detection (see micro-beta-lactamases-esbl-cpe).

objectives: Choose tissue over a surface swab for an infected wound, and say what the evidence shows each yields and costs.
Recognise Pseudomonas aeruginosa from bench clues, and name the organisms listed for puncture wounds.
Explain inducible chromosomal AmpC, name the organisms at highest risk, and choose therapy accordingly.

scenes.title: Three wound-and-blood problems
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three requests on one shift. (1) An infected diabetic foot ulcer arrives with a surface swab only, taken by rubbing the open ulcer. (2) A teenager stepped on a nail through a trainer; the foot now hurts deep over the bone. (3) An Enterobacter cloacae blood isolate was reported ceftriaxone-susceptible, and on day 5 of ceftriaxone the patient is still bacteraemic. Question token: “Which specimen, which organism, which drug?”

cues.text: Three requests on one shift. An infected diabetic foot ulcer arrives with nothing but a swab rubbed across the open ulcer.
A teenager stepped on a nail through a trainer, and the foot now hurts deep over the bone.
And an Enterobacter cloacae blood isolate was called ceftriaxone-susceptible, yet on day five of ceftriaxone the patient is still bacteraemic. Which specimen, which organism, which drug?

props.label: Which specimen, which organism, which drug?

scenes.title: Sample deep, then read the plate
scenes.altText: Four cards. Specimen card: in the CODIFI study of 400 patients with suspected infected diabetic foot ulcers, at least one potential pathogen was reported from 86.1% of tissue samples versus 70.1% of wound swabs taken by Levine’s technique; results differed in 58% of patients, with more pathogens and fewer contaminants from tissue. Bone card: in a review of acute haematogenous osteomyelitis in children, bone or joint samples are culture-positive in about 40–50% of cases versus 10–40% for blood cultures, and samples are best taken before antibiotics where feasible. Puncture-wound card: the same review lists Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa for puncture wounds. Pseudomonas bench card: an aerobic, oxidase-positive gram-negative rod that cannot ferment sugars, with a flower-like or grape-juice odour, beta-haemolysis on blood agar, and pigments — pyoverdine in 70–80% of isolates, plus pyocyanin, pyorubin and pyomelanin.

cues.text: Start with the specimen. In a study of four hundred patients with suspected infected diabetic foot ulcers, tissue samples reported a potential pathogen in eighty-six percent, against seventy percent for swabs taken by Levine technique.

Results differed in fifty-eight percent of patients, with more pathogens and fewer contaminants from tissue. In childhood bone infection, bone or joint cultures are positive in about forty to fifty percent of cases, against ten to forty percent for blood cultures, and are best taken before antibiotics where feasible.
For a puncture wound, the same review of childhood bone infection lists two organisms: Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

Pseudomonas aeruginosa is an oxidase-positive gram-negative rod that cannot ferment sugars. Quick clues are a flower-like or grape-juice odour, beta-haemolysis, and pigments, with the green-yellow pyoverdine in seventy to eighty percent of isolates.

scenes.title: The AmpC spring, and who really has it
scenes.altText: Schematic of chromosomal AmpC regulation: AmpR normally holds ampC expression very low; cell-wall degradation products rise during beta-lactam exposure and AmpD cleaves residues off them; mutations in regulatory genes — ampD more often than ampR, then ampG — allow stable derepression. Risk card: Enterobacter species and Klebsiella aerogenes are the most problematic for AmpC induction; in the larger observational studies summarised by the primer, 3–21% of patients treated with an expanded-spectrum cephalosporin for a susceptible Enterobacter isolate developed resistance on therapy, so expanded-spectrum cephalosporins are best avoided in serious Enterobacter infection even when susceptible in vitro. Contrast card: derepressed Serratia marcescens, Morganella morganii and Providencia stuartii express AmpC about ten-fold lower than derepressed Enterobacter cloacae or Citrobacter freundii; the primer judges AmpC less prominent in the other SPACE organisms and calls it reasonable to base their treatment on in vitro susceptibility; Acinetobacter baumannii carries noninducible chromosomal resistance; Pseudomonas aeruginosa has inducible chromosomal ampC but lies outside the primer’s Enterobacterales-focused treatment advice.

cues.text: Now the resistance. Chromosomal AmpC is a spring held down. The regulator AmpR keeps expression very low, and AmpD trims the cell-wall fragments that build up when certain beta-lactams are given.
Mutations in the regulatory genes, most often ampD, then ampR, then ampG, let the spring stay up even without the drug: stable derepression.

Enterobacter species and Klebsiella aerogenes are the most problematic for induction. In the larger studies, three to twenty-one percent of patients given an expanded-spectrum cephalosporin for a susceptible Enterobacter isolate developed resistance, so those drugs are best avoided in serious Enterobacter infection even when the report says susceptible.

The rest of the SPACE list is not the same. Derepressed Serratia, Morganella and Providencia make about ten times less AmpC than Enterobacter cloacae or Citrobacter freundii, and the primer calls it reasonable to treat the other SPACE organisms by the susceptibility report. Acinetobacter baumannii resistance is not inducible, and Pseudomonas falls outside that treatment advice.

scenes.title: Choosing the drug, and the hook
scenes.altText: Cefepime card: a net neutral charge and low affinity with limited turnover by class C enzymes generally keep cefepime stable against AmpC; it is preferentially given every 8 hours, since 12-hourly dosing allowed Enterobacter cloacae mutant selection in an in vitro model; cefepime resistance, when it appears, is most often from porin mutations, and high organism burden has produced an inoculum effect in vitro. Alternatives card: observational data suggest piperacillin–tazobactam and cefepime are both acceptable for invasive AmpC-producing infections, with more data supporting cefepime, though the question is largely unsettled; convincing clinical data that carbapenems are superior are lacking, though a carbapenem can be reasonable case by case in a severely ill patient with a complex focus. Hook answers: (1) ask for a tissue sample instead of the surface swab; (2) expect Staphylococcus aureus or Pseudomonas aeruginosa and take bone and blood samples before antibiotics where feasible; (3) the Enterobacter cloacae is a derepression risk, so move off ceftriaxone to cefepime or piperacillin–tazobactam.

cues.text: Which drug then? Cefepime is neutral in charge and class C enzymes bind it poorly and turn it over slowly, so it generally stays stable against AmpC. Give it every eight hours: twelve-hourly dosing let Enterobacter cloacae mutants be selected in a laboratory model.
When cefepime does fail, the usual cause is a porin mutation, and a very high organism load has produced an inoculum effect in the laboratory.

Observational data suggest piperacillin and tazobactam is also acceptable for invasive AmpC infections, though more data support cefepime. Carbapenems have not been shown to be superior, but one can be reasonable case by case in a severely ill patient with a complex focus.

Back to the hook. Ask for a tissue sample instead of the surface swab. For the puncture wound, expect Staphylococcus aureus or Pseudomonas aeruginosa and take bone and blood samples before antibiotics where feasible. And move the Enterobacter cloacae patient off ceftriaxone.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “A swab of the open ulcer is as good as tissue” (✓ tissue reported pathogens more often, 86% versus 70%, and fewer contaminants); “Every SPACE organism must be treated as cephalosporin-resistant” (✓ the risk is concentrated in Enterobacter species and Klebsiella aerogenes; for the others, treat by the susceptibility report); “No green pigment, so it is not Pseudomonas” (✓ pyoverdine is reported in only 70–80% of isolates, some isolates make red-brown or brown-black pigments, and pigment production depends on the medium).

cues.text: Trap one: a swab of the open ulcer is as good as tissue. No: tissue reported pathogens more often, and fewer contaminants.
Trap two: every SPACE organism must be treated as cephalosporin-resistant. No: the risk is concentrated in Enterobacter species and Klebsiella aerogenes.

Trap three: no green pigment, so it is not Pseudomonas. No: pyoverdine is reported in only seventy to eighty percent of isolates, some make red-brown or brown-black pigments, and the medium affects pigment production.

✗ “All SPACE organisms = cephalosporin-resistant.”

scenes.title: Lid, hinge, spring
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “AmpC is a spring-loaded lid. AmpR is the LID that holds it shut, AmpD is the HINGE that keeps resetting it, and a broken hinge leaves the lid open for good — that is stable derepression. And the specimen rule: dig for the organism, do not wipe for it.” Tokens: lid = AmpR · hinge = AmpD · broken hinge = derepression. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: AmpC is a spring-loaded lid. AmpR is the lid that holds it shut, AmpD is the hinge that keeps resetting it, and a broken hinge leaves the lid open for good. That is stable derepression. And for specimens: dig for the organism, do not wipe for it.

Where it breaks: AmpR is a regulatory protein, not a physical cover, and induction works through cell-wall degradation products rather than a spring; mutations in ampR and ampG also derepress; organisms differ widely in how much AmpC they make; and tissue sampling caused more ulcer pain and bleeding than swabbing, so it is not free.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Tissue, not a surface swab · puncture wound: Staphylococcus aureus or Pseudomonas aeruginosa”, “Oxidase-positive nonfermenter with grape odour: suspect Pseudomonas aeruginosa · AmpC risk is highest for Enterobacter species”.

cues.text: Culture tissue rather than a surface swab, suspect Pseudomonas aeruginosa when an oxidase-positive nonfermenting rod with a grape-juice odour comes from a puncture wound, and treat inducible AmpC as mainly an Enterobacter species and Klebsiella aerogenes problem rather than a property of every organism in the SPACE mnemonic

props.label: Tissue, not a surface swab · puncture wound: S. aureus or P. aeruginosa
Oxidase + nonfermenter, grape odour: suspect P. aeruginosa · AmpC: Enterobacter

explanation.what: Plain language: where you take the sample decides which organisms you find, an open wound carries surface flora that can crowd the report, and some gram-negative organisms can switch on a chromosomal enzyme that destroys cephalosporins while they are being treated. Scientific terms: Levine’s technique, tissue sampling, nonfermenting gram-negative bacilli, cytochrome oxidase, pyoverdine, pyocyanin, chromosomal ampC, AmpR, AmpD, induction, stable derepression, expanded-spectrum cephalosporin, inoculum effect, porin mutation.
explanation.why: A surface swab tends to pick up superficial flora, including colonisers and contaminants, so a report built on one can mislead therapy. And an isolate reported susceptible to a third-generation cephalosporin can still fail if its chromosomal AmpC derepresses on treatment, which is why the organism’s identity, not only its susceptibility report, shapes the drug choice.
explanation.measure: CODIFI (400 patients, suspected infected diabetic foot ulcer): a potential pathogen reported from 86.1% of tissue samples versus 70.1% of Levine swabs, results differing in 58% of patients; bone or joint cultures positive in about 40–50% of childhood acute haematogenous osteomyelitis versus 10–40% for blood cultures; resistance emerging on expanded-spectrum cephalosporin therapy for susceptible Enterobacter isolates in 3–21% across the larger observational studies in the AmpC primer; pyoverdine produced by 70–80% of P. aeruginosa isolates, pyorubin by 2–3%.
explanation.differs: Tissue versus surface swab; the nonfermenting gram-negative bacilli (Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter, Stenotrophomonas), defined by being unable to ferment sugars, versus fermenting organisms; induction (returns to baseline when the drug stops) versus stable derepression (a regulatory mutation); Enterobacter spp. and K. aerogenes versus the other SPACE organisms; cefepime stability versus porin-mediated cefepime resistance.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: pick the right specimen for an infected wound, name the organism behind a puncture wound, or explain why an Enterobacter isolate reported ceftriaxone-susceptible failed on therapy and what to give instead.

mnemonic.text: AmpC is a spring-loaded lid: AmpR is the LID holding it shut, AmpD is the HINGE that keeps resetting it, and a broken hinge leaves the lid open for good — stable derepression. For specimens: dig for the organism, do not wipe for it.
mnemonic.explanation: Separates reversible induction from a regulatory mutation, and keeps the specimen rule attached to it.
mnemonic.limitation: AmpR is a regulatory protein, not a physical cover, and induction works through cell-wall degradation products rather than a spring; ampR and ampG mutations also derepress; organisms differ widely in how much AmpC they make; and tissue sampling caused more ulcer pain and bleeding than swabbing, so the specimen rule is not cost-free.

analogyLimitations: All three hook cases are invented.
Organism, plate and AmpC drawings are schematic cards, not images of cultures.
CODIFI figures come from infected diabetic foot ulcers in England and may not transfer to every wound type.
Bone-culture yields and the puncture-wound organism list come from a review of children, not adults.
Rates of resistance emerging on cephalosporin therapy vary widely across the cited studies, and the AmpC primer dates from 2019; later trial results were not read for this lesson.
takeaway: Culture tissue rather than a surface swab, suspect Pseudomonas aeruginosa when an oxidase-positive nonfermenting rod with a grape-juice odour comes from a puncture wound, and treat inducible AmpC as mainly an Enterobacter species and Klebsiella aerogenes problem rather than a property of every organism in the SPACE mnemonic

questions.stem: Invented scenario: an Enterobacter cloacae bloodstream isolate is reported susceptible to ceftriaxone, but after 5 days of ceftriaxone the patient is still bacteraemic and the repeat isolate is now ceftriaxone-resistant. What best explains this and what is a reasonable next agent?

options.text: Derepression of chromosomal AmpC during therapy; switch to cefepime, preferably every 8 hours
options.rationale: Correct. Enterobacter spp. are the most problematic organisms for AmpC induction, resistance emerged on expanded-spectrum cephalosporin therapy in 3–21% of patients across the larger observational studies, and cefepime generally stays stable against AmpC, with 8-hourly dosing avoiding the mutant selection seen with 12-hourly dosing in an in vitro model.

options.text: Acquisition of an extended-spectrum β-lactamase, which is reversed by adding clavulanate
options.rationale: Incorrect. The picture fits derepression of the chromosomal class C enzyme in Enterobacter on cephalosporin therapy, and amoxicillin–clavulanate is itself listed as a potent AmpC inducer that common AmpC producers hydrolyse, so adding clavulanate is not the fix.

options.text: Laboratory contamination, so the first susceptibility report should simply be repeated
options.rationale: Incorrect. Emergence of resistance during expanded-spectrum cephalosporin therapy for a susceptible Enterobacter isolate is a documented phenomenon, not a reporting artefact.

options.text: A carbapenem is the only option proven superior for AmpC producers
options.rationale: Incorrect. Convincing clinical data that carbapenems are superior to cefepime or piperacillin–tazobactam for AmpC-producing infections are lacking, though a carbapenem can be reasonable case by case in a severely ill patient with a complex focus.

questions.stem: A patient has a suspected infected diabetic foot ulcer. Based on a large study comparing sampling methods, which specimen is more likely to report the pathogens present, with fewer contaminants?

options.text: A tissue sample taken with a sterile curette or scalpel from the ulcer
options.rationale: Correct. In CODIFI, tissue samples reported at least one potential pathogen in 86.1% of patients versus 70.1% for wound swabs, with more pathogens and fewer non-pathogens reported.

options.text: A wound swab of the ulcer surface
options.rationale: Incorrect. Levine-technique swabs reported pathogens less often and non-pathogens more often than tissue, and blinded clinicians recommended a change of antibiotics less often on swab results; swabs still reported a pathogen in 70.1%, so they are a weaker, not a useless, specimen.

options.text: No culture is needed, because swab and tissue results agree in nearly all patients
options.rationale: Incorrect. Pathogen results differed between the two sampling methods in 58% of patients in CODIFI.

options.text: Blood cultures alone, since they are less invasive than tissue sampling
options.rationale: Incorrect. Blood cultures do not sample the ulcer itself, and where bone is infected (data from children) they are positive less often than bone or joint samples, about 10–40% versus 40–50%.

questions.stem: A gram-negative rod from a puncture wound has a flower-like, grape-juice odour and no visible green pigment. Which finding places it in the nonfermenting gram-negative bacilli, the group that includes Pseudomonas aeruginosa?

options.text: A positive oxidase test in an isolate that does not ferment sugars
options.rationale: Correct. The nonfermenting gram-negative bacilli are defined by being unable to ferment sugars, most of them are oxidase-positive, and P. aeruginosa is described as an oxidase-positive lactose non-fermenter.

options.text: The absence of green pigment, which excludes Pseudomonas
options.rationale: Incorrect. Pyoverdine is reported in only 70–80% of P. aeruginosa isolates, some isolates make red-brown or brown-black pigments, and pigment production depends on the culture medium, so pigment is a supportive clue rather than a requirement.

options.text: The odour alone, which is sufficient for identification
options.rationale: Incorrect. Odour is offered together with beta-haemolysis and colony colour as a quick set of clues, and P. aeruginosa is described by a combination of features (aerobic, motile, oxidase-positive, lactose non-fermenting), so one clue does not carry the identification.

options.text: Fermentation of glucose with acid production
options.rationale: Incorrect. Being unable to ferment sugars is what defines the nonfermenting group, so a fermenting isolate points away from it.

claims.text: Tissue sampling reports pathogens more often and contaminants less often than a Levine-technique wound swab, and is more invasive.
In childhood acute haematogenous osteomyelitis, bone or joint cultures are positive more often than blood cultures, and samples should be taken before antibiotics where feasible.
Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa are the organisms listed for puncture wounds in a paediatric osteomyelitis review.
P. aeruginosa is an oxidase-positive gram-negative rod that cannot ferment sugars, with a grape-juice or flower-like odour, beta-haemolysis and pigments, pyoverdine in 70–80% of isolates.
AmpR holds chromosomal ampC expression low, AmpD trims cell-wall degradation products, and mutations (ampD > ampR > ampG) cause stable derepression.

Enterobacter spp. and K. aerogenes are the highest-risk AmpC organisms (3–21% emergence on expanded-spectrum cephalosporins in the larger studies); derepressed Serratia, Morganella and Providencia make about ten-fold less AmpC, the other SPACE organisms can reasonably be treated by in vitro susceptibility, and A. baumannii chromosomal resistance is noninducible.
Cefepime (every 8 hours) and piperacillin–tazobactam are acceptable for invasive AmpC-producing infections on observational data, with carbapenem superiority unproven.

The reviewer’s specific “sneaker-sole” reservoir for P. aeruginosa in plantar puncture wounds, aspirates as an equivalent specimen to tissue, and the full pathogen-by-site map of Hit 42 (burns, bites, diabetic foot anaerobes).
claims.note: No open source read in this session supports the sneaker-insole reservoir, the aspirate option or the site-by-site pathogen list; only the general puncture-wound association and the swab-versus-tissue comparison were verified.

claims.text: Hook cases invented; plate, organism and AmpC drawings schematic.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 57 Hit 12 tells students to treat all SPACE organisms (Serratia, Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter, Citrobacter, Enterobacter) as resistant to extended-spectrum cephalosporins except cefepime. Tamma 2019 concentrates that risk in Enterobacter spp. and K. aerogenes, reports that derepressed Serratia, Morganella and Providencia express about ten-fold less AmpC than derepressed E. cloacae or C. freundii, states that for the other SPACE organisms it is reasonable to base treatment on in vitro susceptibility, classes Acinetobacter baumannii chromosomal resistance as noninducible, and limits its treatment discussion to Enterobacteriaceae (register flag rv-space-ampc-blanket).

Ch. 57 Hit 42’s “never a surface swab” is stronger than the evidence read here: in CODIFI, Levine-technique swabs still reported at least one potential pathogen in 70.1% of patients (tissue 86.1%), and tissue collection caused more ulcer pain and bleeding, so the choice is method-dependent rather than absolute (register flag rv-wound-swab-levine).

Ch. 57 Hit 26 links a sneaker-sole puncture wound to P. aeruginosa alone; the paediatric review read here lists Staphylococcus aureus as well as P. aeruginosa for puncture wounds, and no source read in this session supports the sneaker-specific association (register flag rv-puncture-two-organisms).

morphology.note: No micrographs or plate photographs; bench clues and AmpC regulation shown as schematic cards.

Independently re-checked: emergence figure corrected from 3–19% to 3–21%. No human expert has reviewed this lesson.
